<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Ablation Studies</h3>

<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Robustness Across Datasets.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to computational constraints, we evaluate hyperparameter robustness on four representative benchmarks: AIME24, AIME25, BRUMO25, and HMMT25 (Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.2.1 Overall Performance ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Empirical and Statistical Evaluation ‣ Thinking by Subtraction: Confidence-Driven Contrastive Decoding for LLM Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
We fix the contrastive decoding threshold <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> and masking threshold <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> to their optimal values on AIME25 and directly apply the same configuration to all other benchmarks without additional tuning.
Across datasets with diverse difficulty levels and reasoning characteristics, CCD consistently improves over the Base method and remains competitive with MTI, indicating that its effectiveness does not rely on dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Robustness of the Thresholds <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{cd}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{cd}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{rep}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{rep}</annotation></semantics></math> Across Model Scales</h5>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate CCD under four representative hyperparameter settings, including <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\tau_{cd},\tau_{rep})=(2,5),(3,5),(3,8),(3,10)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\tau_{cd},\tau_{rep})=(2,5),(3,5),(3,8),(3,10)</annotation></semantics></math>.
As shown in Table <a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Robustness of Token Replacement Strategies. ‣ 3.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 3 Empirical and Statistical Evaluation ‣ Thinking by Subtraction: Confidence-Driven Contrastive Decoding for LLM Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, all evaluated configurations consistently outperform the Base decoding across different model scales on AIME25.
These results indicate that the performance gains of CCD are robust to hyperparameter choices and do not rely on a specific setting.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Robustness of Token Replacement Strategies.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct ablation studies to evaluate the robustness of the token replacement strategies used to construct the contrastive reference distribution.
Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Robustness of Token Replacement Strategies. ‣ 3.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 3 Empirical and Statistical Evaluation ‣ Thinking by Subtraction: Confidence-Driven Contrastive Decoding for LLM Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> examines the effect of varying replacement intervals.
Replacing high-confidence tokens consistently induces a more uncertain (higher-entropy) contrastive distribution compared to replacing mid- or low-confidence tokens.
Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Robustness of Token Replacement Strategies. ‣ 3.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 3 Empirical and Statistical Evaluation ‣ Thinking by Subtraction: Confidence-Driven Contrastive Decoding for LLM Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> further studies different placeholder choices, showing that semantically minimal symbols yield the most stable and effective contrastive signal.
These results demonstrate that the proposed replacement strategy is robust to threshold selection and provides a principled foundation for confidence-driven contrastive decoding.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Empirical Analysis</h3>

<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Effect of CCD on Token-Level Confidence.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first examine the effect of CCD on token-level confidence at decoding positions identified as low-confidence in the original decoding branch.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Effect of CCD on Token-Level Confidence. ‣ 3.4 Empirical Analysis ‣ 3 Empirical and Statistical Evaluation ‣ Thinking by Subtraction: Confidence-Driven Contrastive Decoding for LLM Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, CCD consistently increases token-level confidence at these positions after intervention.
Quantitatively, the mean confidence of low-confidence tokens in the original branch increases from <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="6.355" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>6.355</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6.355</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="6.673" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>6.673</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6.673</annotation></semantics></math> after applying CCD.
This improvement indicates that confidence-driven intervention selectively stabilizes previously uncertain decoding steps, rather than uniformly inflating confidence across all tokens.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18232v1/token_conf_c.svg" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/215;" width="476" height="215"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S3.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Token-level confidence improvement at low-confidence decoding positions.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18232v1/base.svg" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/281;" width="476" height="281"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S3.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Trajectory-level confidence comparison before CCD intervention.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18232v1/mean_ccd.svg" id="S3.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/281;" width="476" height="281"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S3.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Trajectory-level confidence comparison after CCD intervention.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Effect of CCD on Trace-Level Confidence.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further analyze how token-level confidence improvements propagate to the trajectory level.
Figures <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Effect of CCD on Token-Level Confidence. ‣ 3.4 Empirical Analysis ‣ 3 Empirical and Statistical Evaluation ‣ Thinking by Subtraction: Confidence-Driven Contrastive Decoding for LLM Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Effect of CCD on Token-Level Confidence. ‣ 3.4 Empirical Analysis ‣ 3 Empirical and Statistical Evaluation ‣ Thinking by Subtraction: Confidence-Driven Contrastive Decoding for LLM Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> visualize the confidence distributions of complete decoding traces before and after CCD, respectively.
Under the base decoding strategy, correct and incorrect trajectories exhibit substantial overlap, limiting the discriminative power of confidence scores.
After applying CCD, the separability between the two distributions is noticeably improved.
Specifically, the mean confidence of correct trajectories increases from <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18.89" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>18.89</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18.89</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18.98" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>18.98</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18.98</annotation></semantics></math>, while the mean confidence of incorrect trajectories decreases from <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15.25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>15.25</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15.25</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="14.70" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>14.70</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">14.70</annotation></semantics></math>.
These results demonstrate that CCD not only stabilizes local token-level uncertainty, but also enhances trace-level confidence separation, yielding a more reliable confidence signal for downstream verification and reranking.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Effect of CCD on Reasoning Length and Efficiency</h5>

<figure id="S3.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18232v1/length.svg" id="S3.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/187;" width="476" height="187"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="S3.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Average response length of the base output, CCD output, and contrastive distribution for Qwen3-8B across benchmarks.
CCD substantially shortens responses on AIME-style tasks while preserving response length on HMMT25 and BRUMO25, whereas the contrastive distribution yields consistently longer outputs.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18232v1/phrase.svg" id="S3.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/187;" width="476" height="187"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="S3.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Frequency of explicit thinking tokens in model responses for Qwen3-8B.
CCD significantly reduces thinking-token usage on AIME benchmarks while leaving HMMT25 and BRUMO25 largely unchanged, indicating selective suppression of overextended reasoning.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the effect of CCD on reasoning length and efficiency by comparing the response length and the frequency of explicit thinking tokens across datasets.
Figure <a href="#S3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Effect of CCD on Reasoning Length and Efficiency ‣ 3.4 Empirical Analysis ‣ 3 Empirical and Statistical Evaluation ‣ Thinking by Subtraction: Confidence-Driven Contrastive Decoding for LLM Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> reports the average response length for the base distribution, the final CCD output, and the contrastive distribution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">On AIME24 and AIME25, CCD produces substantially shorter responses than the base method.
This reduction indicates that CCD encourages more compact reasoning trajectories, effectively removing redundant or unnecessary intermediate steps.
In contrast, the responses generated from the contrastive distribution are significantly longer, reflecting the higher uncertainty and weakened semantic constraints induced by masking.
This clear separation confirms that CCD sharpens the final prediction by subtracting a deliberately confused reference distribution rather than truncating reasoning arbitrarily.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On HMMT25 and BRUMO25, the response lengths of the base and CCD outputs largely overlap.
This behavior suggests that CCD does not disrupt stable reasoning patterns when the model is already confident, preserving the original reasoning structure on datasets that do not exhibit strong overthinking.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Effect of CCD on Reasoning Length and Efficiency ‣ 3.4 Empirical Analysis ‣ 3 Empirical and Statistical Evaluation ‣ Thinking by Subtraction: Confidence-Driven Contrastive Decoding for LLM Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> further analyzes the frequency of explicit thinking tokens.
On AIME-style benchmarks, CCD significantly reduces the occurrence of such tokens, especially on AIME25, indicating a reduction in repetitive or unproductive deliberation.
In contrast, thinking-token frequency remains nearly unchanged on HMMT25 and BRUMO25, demonstrating that CCD maintains strong stability and avoids unnecessary intervention.
Together, these results show that CCD improves reasoning efficiency by selectively compressing overextended reasoning while leaving confident reasoning trajectories intact.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Conclusion and Limitations</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we investigate how token-level predictive confidence can be exploited as a decoding-time control signal for improving large language model reasoning.
We propose <em id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Confidence-Driven Contrastive Decoding</em> (CCD), a simple yet principled approach that performs selective contrastive subtraction at locally unstable decoding states.
Extensive experiments on multiple competitive mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that CCD consistently improves reasoning accuracy across diverse model scales, without requiring additional training or multiple inference trajectories.
These results suggest that uncertainty-aware decoding offers an efficient alternative to conventional test-time scaling strategies based on extensive sampling or trajectory expansion, achieving a favorable efficiency–performance trade-off with negligible overhead.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Despite these promising results, our study has several limitations.
Due to computational constraints, our evaluation primarily focuses on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, which, while standard for assessing structured multi-step reasoning, do not fully capture the diversity of real-world reasoning tasks.
The effectiveness of CCD on more general-domain benchmarks therefore remains to be systematically explored.
In addition, our experiments are limited to text-only large language models.
Extending CCD to multimodal reasoning settings, such as models jointly processing text and vision, is a natural and promising direction for future work, where token-level confidence may interact with modality-specific representations in more complex ways.
We hope this work encourages further investigation into confidence-guided decoding strategies as a lightweight and broadly applicable approach to enhancing LLM reasoning reliability.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work proposes Confidence-Driven Contrastive Decoding (CCD) to improve the reliability of large language models in reasoning tasks by mitigating erroneous or low-confidence token generation. While CCD aims to enhance model robustness and reduce reasoning failures, it may still inherit biases present in the underlying pre-trained models and datasets, potentially leading to uneven performance across domains or problem types. Moreover, as with other advanced reasoning techniques, improved reasoning capability could be misused to generate more convincing but incorrect or misleading content if deployed irresponsibly. From a societal perspective, CCD has the potential to improve the dependability of LLM-based systems in high-stakes applications such as education, scientific assistance, and decision support, where reducing unreliable reasoning is particularly important.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Related Works</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Test-Time Scaling</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Test-time scaling (TTS) enhances LLM reasoning by increasing computational budget during inference rather than training. A prominent line of work focuses on <em id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">parallel scaling</em>, which generates multiple reasoning trajectories and aggregates them through majority voting or reward models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. However, these methods often suffer from diminishing returns as the number of samples increases, and incur prohibitive computational overhead due to sampling numerous complete reasoning paths <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lightman et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recent efforts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025c</a>)</cite> enhance inference efficiency via training-based interventions that reshape decoding behavior, leading to shorter reasoning trajectories and reduced autoregressive length. DeepConf <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> employs model-internal confidence signals to dynamically filter low-quality reasoning traces during or after generation, achieving significant token reduction while maintaining accuracy.
Other approaches, such as adaptive consistency methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ammar, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Taubenfeld et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, aim to determine the optimal number of reasoning chains without exhaustive sampling.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike these methods that inherently require multiple inference passes to scale performance, our approach demonstrates that effective test-time improvement can be achieved through <em id="A1.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">single-pass</em> selective intervention on critical tokens, eliminating the need for multiple reasoning trajectories entirely. This distinguishes our method from both parallel scaling (which samples multiple trajectories) and sequential scaling (which iteratively refines a single trajectory through self-correction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madaan et al., 2023</a>)</cite>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Uncertainty Estimation in LLMs</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Uncertainty estimation has become an important tool for improving the reliability of large language model (LLM) generation.
Existing approaches can be broadly categorized into <em id="A1.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">entropy-based</em> and <em id="A1.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">confidence-based</em> methods.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Entropy-based methods</span> identify uncertain positions using token-level entropy.
Prior studies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> demonstrate that reasoning uncertainty is highly localized, with a small subset of high-entropy tokens disproportionately influencing output correctness, motivating selective intervention at these positions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Confidence-based methods</span> leverage the model’s predictive confidence as a direct indicator of uncertainty to optimize both model learning and execution. On the learning side, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2025a)</a></cite> introduce a reinforcement learning fine-tuning framework that utilizes confidence signals to guide few-shot policy optimization. In contrast, for inference-time control, recent works such as DeepConf <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Taubenfeld et al. (2025)</a></cite>, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2026)</a></cite> employ confidence to dynamically modulate the decoding process, ensuring greater reasoning reliability without additional training.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast to entropy-based approaches, our work adopts token-level predictive confidence as the uncertainty measure and directly leverages it to perform trajectory correction during decoding.
By intervening at low-confidence positions and refining the decoding trajectory accordingly, our method provides a simple and effective confidence-guided mechanism for improving reasoning reliability.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Contrastive Decoding</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Contrastive Decoding (CD) improves generation quality by contrasting the output distributions of different models or different prompting conditions. This paradigm has been applied across both text-only and multimodal settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Text-based CD methods</span> originated with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2023)</a></cite>, who contrast larger models against smaller amateur models to improve factuality. Subsequent work extended this paradigm: DoLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chuang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> contrasts logits between different transformer layers to mitigate hallucinations; ICD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> induces hallucinations through lightweight fine-tuning to create a ”weak” model for contrast, penalizing fabricated information during decoding; and ACD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> employs opposite prompt optimization to boost safety alignment through adversarial contrast.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multimodal CD methods</span> address hallucinations in vision-language models (VLMs). VCD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leng et al., 2024</a>)</cite> contrasts distributions between original and visually perturbed inputs to reduce object hallucinations. While these methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> require auxiliary models, layer-wise computations, or multiple forward passes, our approach distinguishes itself by performing <em id="A1.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">localized</em> contrastive intervention only at high-uncertainty tokens, significantly reducing computational overhead while maintaining or improving effectiveness across both textual and reasoning tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Appendix.</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Case Study: Qualitative Comparison of Reasoning Traces</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present a qualitative case study on an AIME 2025 combinatorics problem to illustrate how Confidence-Driven Contrastive Decoding (CCD) affects the reasoning process compared to standard chain-of-thought decoding.
Figure shows a side-by-side comparison between a Trivial CoT trace generated by the base decoding strategy and a CoT trace produced by CCD.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F9" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A2.F9.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="237.1" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 237.1" width="477.38"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,237.1) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 231.19 C 0 234.45 2.64 237.1 5.91 237.1 L 471.47 237.1 C 474.73 237.1 477.38 234.45 477.38 231.19 L 477.38 5.91 C 477.38 2.64 474.73 0 471.47 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 216.36 L 475.41 216.36 L 475.41 5.91 C 475.41 3.73 473.65 1.97 471.47 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 6.12 224.36)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:42.17em;--ltx-fo-height:0.6em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.17em;font-size:7.97pt;" height="8.5" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 6.62)" width="465.19"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:42.17em;">
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F9.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Comparing Reasoning Outputs on AIME2025</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 6.12 6.12)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:42.17em;--ltx-fo-height:18.68em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:7.97pt;" height="206.09" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 206.09)" width="465.19"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="A2.F9.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:42.17em;">
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F9.pic1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Problem.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F9.pic1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The twelve letters <math id="A2.F9.pic1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>,<math id="A2.F9.pic1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>,<math id="A2.F9.pic1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">E</mi><annotation class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math>,<math id="A2.F9.pic1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math>,<math id="A2.F9.pic1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math>,<math id="A2.F9.pic1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A2.F9.pic1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> are randomly grouped into six pairs of letters.
The two letters in each pair are placed next to each other in alphabetical order to form six two-letter words, and then those six words are listed alphabetically.
For example, a possible result is <math id="A2.F9.pic1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="AB" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">AB</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.F9.pic1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="CJ" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">J</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">CJ</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.F9.pic1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="DG" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">G</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">DG</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.F9.pic1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="EK" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">E</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">EK</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.F9.pic1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="FL" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi encoding="application/x-tex">FL</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.F9.pic1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="HI" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">H</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">I</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">HI</annotation></semantics></math>.
The probability that the last word listed contains <math id="A2.F9.pic1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="A2.F9.pic1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{m}{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000"><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">m</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">n</mi></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{m}{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A2.F9.pic1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.F9.pic1.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> are relatively prime positive integers.
Find <math id="A2.F9.pic1.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m+n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">m</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">+</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m+n</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A2.F9.pic1.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" color="#000000" height="55.53" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 465.14 55.53" width="465.14"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,55.53) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 49.62 C 0 52.88 2.64 55.53 5.91 55.53 L 459.23 55.53 C 462.49 55.53 465.14 52.88 465.14 49.62 L 465.14 5.91 C 465.14 2.64 462.49 0 459.23 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 36.56 L 463.17 36.56 L 463.17 5.91 C 463.17 3.73 461.41 1.97 459.23 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 6.12 42.68)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:41.06em;--ltx-fo-height:0.61em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:7.97pt;" height="6.73" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 6.73)" width="452.95"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p2.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:41.06em;">
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p2.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F9.pic1.p2.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Trival CoT</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 6.12 25.15)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:41.06em;--ltx-fo-height:0.66em;--ltx-fo-depth:1.72em;font-size:7.97pt;" height="26.29" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 7.26)" width="452.95"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p2.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:41.06em;">
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p2.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F9.pic1.p2.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">“…
Therefore, given that all approaches lead to <math id="A2.F9.pic1.p2.pic1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40/231" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">40</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">/</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">231</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40/231</annotation></semantics></math>, I think that is the correct answer.
Therefore, the probability is <math id="A2.F9.pic1.p2.pic1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40/231" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">40</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">/</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">231</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40/231</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math id="A2.F9.pic1.p2.pic1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m+n=40+231=271" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">m</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">+</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">n</mi></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">=</mo><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">40</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">+</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">231</mn></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;" mathcolor="#FF0000">271</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m+n=40+231=271</annotation></semantics></math>.”</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</span>
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A2.F9.pic1.p3.pic1" class="ltx_picture" color="#000000" height="56.16" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 465.14 56.16" width="465.14"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,56.16) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 50.26 C 0 53.52 2.64 56.16 5.91 56.16 L 459.23 56.16 C 462.49 56.16 465.14 53.52 465.14 50.26 L 465.14 5.91 C 465.14 2.64 462.49 0 459.23 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 37.3 L 463.17 37.3 L 463.17 5.91 C 463.17 3.73 461.41 1.97 459.23 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 6.12 43.42)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:41.06em;--ltx-fo-height:0.6em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:7.97pt;" height="6.62" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 6.62)" width="452.95"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p3.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:41.06em;">
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p3.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F9.pic1.p3.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">CCD CoT</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 6.12 24.61)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:41.06em;--ltx-fo-height:0.77em;--ltx-fo-depth:1.68em;font-size:7.97pt;" height="27.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.55)" width="452.95"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p3.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:41.06em;">
<span id="A2.F9.pic1.p3.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F9.pic1.p3.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#009900;">“…
But let me check if 128 and 693 are coprime.
As before, 128 is <math id="A2.F9.pic1.p3.pic1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{7}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;" mathcolor="#009900">2</mn><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;" mathcolor="#009900">7</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{7}</annotation></semantics></math>, 693 is <math id="A2.F9.pic1.p3.pic1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7\times 9\times 11" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;" mathcolor="#009900">7</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;" lspace="0.222em" mathcolor="#009900" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;" mathcolor="#009900">9</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;" lspace="0.222em" mathcolor="#009900" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;" mathcolor="#009900">11</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7\times 9\times 11</annotation></semantics></math>.
No common factors, so yes.
Therefore, the final answer is <math id="A2.F9.pic1.p3.pic1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="128+693=821" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;" mathcolor="#009900">128</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;" mathcolor="#009900">+</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;" mathcolor="#009900">693</mn></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;" mathcolor="#009900">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;" mathcolor="#009900">821</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">128+693=821</annotation></semantics></math>.”</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</span></span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F9.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="A2.F9.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">
Case study on an AIME 2025 problem: comparison between Trivial CoT and CCD CoT on a combinatorics task.
</span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Discussion: Stability vs. Exploration</h3>

<section id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Stability versus exploration in reasoning.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From a reasoning perspective, effective inference requires balancing two complementary forces:
exploiting strong semantic priors to maintain stability, and selectively relaxing them to allow exploration when uncertainty arises.
CCD primarily targets the stability side of this trade-off.
By suppressing spurious alternatives at low-confidence positions through contrastive subtraction, CCD reduces the risk of error amplification and maintains coherent reasoning trajectories.
This analysis helps explain why CCD yields consistent gains across diverse reasoning benchmarks despite its simplicity.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<th id="A2.T4.5.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row"><span id="A2.T4.5.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Verification</span></th>
<td id="A2.T4.5.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">
<span id="A2.T4.5.6.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="A2.T4.5.6.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">seems solid, Seems solid, that’s correct, but, That’s correct, but, that seems right, That seems right</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T4.5.7" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A2.T4.5.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb"><span id="A2.T4.5.7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Markers</span></th>
<td id="A2.T4.5.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A2.T4.5.7.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="A2.T4.5.7.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">SO</span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
</section>

      methods listed below:</p>

    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
